item.content:encoded:
While presenting at a Princeton conference on the impact fathers have on romantic and sexual relationships, a male student asked me: How do men learn to build healthy, lasting relationships with women?
“I’ve tried hooking up,” he said. “It isn’t working.”
When I shared some basic research on how trust and love are built between two people, I expected hope. Instead, he grew visibly frustrated: “Why has no one ever shown me this?”
“All I’ve ever been shown is sex, with commitment and intimacy being optional,” he continued. “I don’t know anything else, and it isn’t working!”
This young man was right to feel deceived. Modern dating culture routinely promotes physical hookups while skipping the foundations of intimacy and trust, leaving young men and women primed for sex but completely unprepared for long-term, committed love.
Sexually active and profoundly lonely
This is the quiet tragedy beneath a very loud national conversation. Was this student an outlier? Or was he simply honest enough to say out loud what many of his peers are feeling?
Since that day, I have heard numerous versions of his frustration from students on campuses across the country. They are bright, ambitious and sexually liberated … or so they’ve been told.
Yet many of them are silently lonely. Ironically, a generation raised on the promise of sexual freedom often finds itself less free to build the very relationships it most wants.
An ‘old-fashioned’ idea
Saying the word “chastity” on most college campuses today is likely to result in laughter, mocking or even contempt. For many in the Western world, it sounds hopelessly behind the times — a prudish list of restrictive “don’ts” handed down from a repressive age.
But this caricatures a profoundly rich idea. At its heart, chastity is not merely the absence of sex before marriage. It is a vision of what sex is for: the conviction that physical intimacy belongs within a relationship of trust, commitment and genuinely knowing another person. Chastity is where two people seek each other’s good, not just each other’s consent.
Chastity is not the enemy of love. It is love’s partner and protector. And contrary to popular perception, this timeless truth is as needed as ever.
Chastity is where two people seek each other’s good, not just each other’s consent.
In “How to Avoid Falling in Love with a Jerk,” John Van Epp identifies five areas that build deep attachments between two people: knowing, trusting, relying on, committing to and touching one another. Healthy relationships build these bonds in that order, and the rule is simple: never go further in one area than you have in the one before it.
Hookup culture makes a mess out of this sequence, elevating touch first, the deepest bond of all, which can give both parties a false sense of knowing and trusting each other while leaving reliance and commitment optional. Through this lens, we see that chastity isn’t arbitrary or naive. It honors the order in which love is actually built.
Consent is essential, but it’s a floor, not a ceiling
One of the groups best positioned to hand a healthier sexual script to the next generation is fathers. But their message needs to go beyond “Make sure she says yes.”
Consent, of course, is essential. Columnist Christine Emba insightfully described consent as “the floor,” the minimum that separates a sexual encounter from a crime.
But a floor is not a ceiling. Consent can tell us whether something was a violation. It cannot tell us whether it was good, wise, loving or dignifying. A culture that knows how to ask only “Was there consent?” has forgotten how to ask everything that sits above it, including intimacy, trust, commitment, sacrifice and dare I say: love.
“As long as both consent” is the sexual script the Princeton students had been handed. They were given the floor and told it was the whole house.
Consent can tell us whether something was a violation. It cannot tell us whether it was good, wise, loving or dignifying.
The consent conundrum
One detail from the recent Cornell sexual assault lawsuit was especially disturbing. In the early morning hours, one of the men allegedly posted to the fraternity’s group chat that sex was available upstairs, using words too crude to print here. He described the young woman as “free.”
It is hard to imagine a darker distortion of the freedom the sexual revolution promised. A message like that is a failure of more than consent ethics — seeing a young woman not as a person to be known, protected or honored but as an available commodity.
On social media, dads are asking why not one of the seven young men had the guts to respond, “No! That is not how we treat a woman!”
Questions about consent, burden of proof and accountability are important. But they are all about the floor — asking whether a line was crossed. None of them asks why a group of bright young men at an Ivy League school would see a young woman that way in the first place.
While there are many influences on perception, the widespread use of pornography among young men is hard to ignore. Research on fraternity members finds that those who view pornography are significantly less likely to step in to stop a sexual assault.
Tragically, whether we like it or not, pornography has become sex education for a generation, with the power to shape developing minds and hearts.
Dad power
Courts can punish and Title IX offices can sanction, but neither can shape a young man’s heart. That work happens much earlier and ideally much closer to home.
The father-son relationship may be one of the most overlooked tools we have for preventing sexual violence. The presence and warmth of a father growing up is one of the strongest predictors of how a man handles his emotions, including aggression and how he treats women.
A boy learns what a man does with his strength, his desire and his power by watching the man closest to him. Does Dad speak of women with respect or with lust and contempt? Does he honor his wife or use and mistreat her? Does he show his son that real men protect the vulnerable rather than exploit them?
Sons are watching, and they are taking notes long before they are old enough to join a fraternity. That’s where a young man’s moral intuitions are formed — not in a mandatory university orientation session at age 18.
Mothers, of course, also have an enormous influence on sons. And the father-daughter relationship carries its own enormous potential. Wake Forest psychologist Linda Nielsen says a father has “the greater influence on his daughter’s ability to trust, enjoy and relate well to the men in her life.” Young women whose fathers were highly involved tend to report more intimacy, commitment and trust in their own romantic relationships.
None of these findings places the burden of preventing assault on young women. Responsibility for sexual violence and exploitation belongs entirely to those who commit it. But a daughter who knows her worth from the inside out, because she has been loved well by the first man in her life, is more likely to have emotionally fulfilling relationships and to recognize real love when it comes.
Show them how
Fathers can teach a better way, but first and foremost, they have to live it. Children absorb what they see long before they understand what they hear. A father who builds genuine trust and commitment with their mother earns the credibility to explain why it matters. More than just words, his life becomes the lesson. So fathers, two big things you can do:
- Treat your children’s mother, and every woman, with respect. Your sons and daughters are learning what love looks like by watching you.
- Show your daughters in words, time and attention that they are loved unconditionally and deserve to be treated with dignity.
Also, be a father figure to those who don’t have one. Fatherlessness, the absence of men who model and teach a better way, has left a generation to learn about love from a script written by the culture rather than the home.
It’s been said that a society can have sexual freedom or strong families, but not both. Consent and law enforcement will always matter, but they are the floor — not the whole house.
There’s a much bigger, more beautiful picture for our children to understand. And that’s on us as parents. Let’s make sure no child of ours ever has to ask, “Why has no one ever shown me this?”
